ginebra-san-miguel: Ginebra San Miguel traces its beginnings to 1834, when the Manila trading house that became Ayala y Compañía opened the Destilería Ayala, by many accounts the first distillery in the Philippines, whose gins came to include Ginebra San Miguel. In 1924 the distillery and its brands were bought by La Tondeña, the company Carlos Palanca had founded in Tondo, and San Miguel Corporation took over that business in 1987. The label of Saint Michael defeating the devil, which earned the bottle the nickname Marca Demonio, is credited to Fernando Amorsolo, later the country's first National Artist.
philippine-rum: Philippine rum is dominated by Tanduay, which dates itself to 1854, the founding year of the Manila trading house Ynchausti y Compañía. The firm bought a working distillery in Hagonoy, Bulacan, in 1856 and later set up a plant on Isla de Tanduay in Manila, the spot that gave the rum its name. Elizalde & Company took over the distillery in the 1930s, and in 1988 the brand passed to a company owned by the businessman Lucio Tan, under whom it grew into one of the largest rum brands in the world.
lao-khao: Lao khao, whose name simply means white liquor, is Thailand's everyday spirit of rice or molasses, made by licensed distilleries and in villages across the country with no single recorded beginning.
mekhong: Mekhong was launched in 1941 by Thailand's Excise Department and made at the state-run Bangyikhan Distillery outside Bangkok, which the government had taken over in 1914. Its name, after the Mekong river along the border with Laos, was chosen while Thailand was in dispute with French Indochina over that very border, and the same distillery still makes it.
ya-dong: Ya dong is the Thai custom of steeping lao khao with roots, barks and herbs in big glass jars and selling it by the glass at roadside stalls, a folk practice with no recorded origin.
thai-rum: Thai rum in the French island style is recent, and its best-known name is Chalong Bay on Phuket, founded in 2012 by Marine Lucchini and Thibault Spithakis, a French couple. They set out to bring the French Caribbean practice of distilling fresh cane juice, rather than molasses, to Thai sugarcane, and named the rum after Chalong Bay in the south of the island.
ruou-de: Rượu đế is the village rice spirit of Vietnam, distilled in the Mekong delta and the north since before anyone recorded it. Its name is usually explained by the French colonial alcohol monopoly, which made village distilling illegal: distillers are said to have hidden their stills among đế, a tall wild grass, and the word stuck to the spirit itself.
ruou-thuoc: Rượu thuốc, medicine liquor, is the Vietnamese practice of steeping rice spirit with roots, herbs and sometimes animals, a household and village tradition with no recorded beginning.
vietnamese-gin: Vietnamese gin as a category was opened by Sông Cái Distillery, founded in 2018 by Daniel Nguyen, who grew up in Southern California and had worked on rural development programmes in Vietnam before turning to spirits. Its name, Sông Cái, means mother river and is an old name for the Red River. The gin is built around wild botanicals bought from foragers and farmers in the northern highlands, among them Red Dao and Hmong families in Lào Cai province, an approach meant to add value to plants those communities already know.
sraa-sar: Sraa sar, white spirit in Khmer, is Cambodia's rice spirit, made in homes and villages across the country by a tradition with no recorded beginning.
sombai: Sombai was founded in Siem Reap in 2012 by Joëlle Jean-Louis and Lionel Maitrepierre, who built it on sraa tram, the Cambodian custom of steeping rice spirit with fruit, herbs and roots. Each bottle is hand-painted by local artists, and the decoration has become as much a part of the product as the liqueur inside.
lao-lao: Lao-lao is the sticky rice spirit of Laos, distilled in villages along the Mekong and poured at Lao celebrations, with no recorded beginning.
htan-yay-a-yet: Htan yay a-yet is the toddy palm spirit of Myanmar's dry zone around Bagan, distilled from fermented palm sap by village families in a tradition with no recorded beginning.
myanmar-rum: Myanmar rum is molasses rum distilled from the country's own sugarcane and rarely exported, and its beginnings are not well documented.
samsu: Samsu is the Malayan form of samshu, the name European traders in China gave to Chinese distilled spirit, a word of debated origin traced either to a Cantonese phrase meaning thrice-fired or to shaojiu, burnt liquor. In colonial Singapore and the other Straits Settlements the right to make and sell spirits was let out as a revenue farm, usually to Chinese merchant syndicates, and samsu has remained the region's cheap everyday spirit ever since.
singapore-gin: The Singapore gin category is usually traced to Jamie Koh, who opened Brass Lion Distillery in 2018, billed as the city's first standalone craft distillery, after training as a distiller in the United States and Germany. Its gins lean on Southeast Asian botanicals rather than the classic European set, giving the home of the Singapore Sling a gin of its own.
tua-sabu: Tua sabu is the distilled palm spirit of Timor-Leste, made in villages from the sap of lontar and coconut palms and poured at customary ceremonies, with no recorded beginning.
australian-whisky: Australia's modern whisky story is usually dated to 1992, when Bill and Lyn Lark gained the first distilling licence in Tasmania since 1839, after persuading the federal government to change a rule in the Distillation Act that barred small stills. Distilling had been banned on the island under Governor John Franklin, and the Larks showed that Tasmanian barley, peat and water could make malt whisky. Dozens of distilleries followed, and in 2014 a single cask of Sullivans Cove French Oak was named World's Best Single Malt, the first winner from outside Scotland and Japan.
australian-rum: Beenleigh, on the Albert River south of Brisbane, became a rum distillery in 1884, when Francis Gooding, co-owner of the local sugar plantation, bought the still of the Walrus, a boat that had worked the district's rivers as a floating mill and distillery. Bundaberg Distilling Company was formed in 1888 to make use of the molasses the local sugar mills were left with, and distilled its first rum the next year. Rum had been part of Australian life since the colony's earliest days, when the overthrow of Governor William Bligh in 1808 came to be called the Rum Rebellion.
australian-gin: Australia had few gin distillers until the 2010s, when a wave of small producers turned to native botanicals and made gin one of the country's busiest craft categories. Its best-known name, Four Pillars, was founded in 2013 in the Yarra Valley by Cameron Mackenzie, Stuart Gregor and Matt Jones, and its Bloody Shiraz Gin, first released in 2015, is made by steeping whole shiraz grapes in gin until it turns a deep purple.
bush-tucker-liqueur: Bush tucker liqueurs are a modern Australian style built on native fruits such as Davidson plum and quandong, made by many small producers and with no single recorded inventor.
new-zealand-whisky: New Zealand's modern whisky story runs through the Willowbank distillery in Dunedin, where production began in 1974. Seagram bought it in the 1980s and sold its single malts as Lammerlaw, but after Foster's took over it was closed in 1997, its stills were shipped to Fiji to make rum, and the remaining casks ended up with The New Zealand Whisky Company, which has released them slowly from a warehouse in Oamaru. A new generation of distilleries has since started again from scratch.
hokonui-moonshine: Hokonui moonshine is named for the Hokonui Hills near Gore in Southland, where the family of Mary McRae, who had come from the Scottish Highlands with seven children in 1872, is remembered for running the district's best-known illegal still in the nineteenth century. Demand grew after the Mataura district, which included Gore, voted itself dry at the start of the twentieth century, and the McRaes and others kept distilling in the hills for decades, until local prohibition was lifted half a century later. Gore's Hokonui Moonshine Museum now tells the story.
new-zealand-gin: New Zealand gin is a young craft category with no single founding story, built by small distilleries around native plants such as horopito, kawakawa and mānuka.
feijoa-liqueur: Feijoa liqueur is a New Zealand fruit liqueur with no recorded inventor, made from the South American feijoa that New Zealand gardens took up in the twentieth century.
fijian-rum: Fiji's rum comes from the distillery at Lautoka, set up in 1980 as South Pacific Distilleries to turn the country's molasses into spirit. Foster's later bought it and installed pot stills from its closed Willowbank whisky distillery in New Zealand, which run beside a column still. Long known at home for Bounty rum, the distillery was renamed the Rum Co. of Fiji in 2015 and launched the Ratu and Bati ranges, while its rums have also been bottled abroad by independent blenders.
rhum-de-tahiti: Rhum de Tahiti is French Polynesia's agricole rum, distilled in small quantities from fresh cane juice grown on Tahiti and Taha'a in the French island tradition, with no well-documented origin story.
hawaiian-rum: Hawaiian rum as a craft is young: Kōloa Rum Company on Kauai was founded in 2009, and Kō Hana on Oahu made its first agricole-style rum in 2014 from heirloom Hawaiian cane, varieties said to descend from those the first Polynesian voyagers brought to the islands. The sugar plantations dominated Hawaii for well over a century, until the last mill, at Puunene on Maui, closed in 2016, leaving rum makers to grow or source their cane on a small scale.
steamit: Steamit is the home-distilled spirit of Papua New Guinea, made from whatever will ferment in improvised stills, an informal practice with no recorded beginning.
clarito: The Clarito is credited to Santiago 'Pichín' Policastro, a Buenos Aires bartender and the son of Italian immigrants, who wrote that he created it in 1935 as a very dry gin Martini crowned with a rim of lemon and sugar. Policastro won an international cocktail competition in Bern in 1954 with another drink, El Pato, and published the cocktail book Tragos mágicos the following year. The Clarito was popular in the 1930s, then faded until Buenos Aires bartenders revived it in the 2000s, mostly without the sugar rim.
gancia-batido: The Gancia batido is an Argentine way of serving Gancia, the Italian aperitif, shaken with lemon and sugar, a café and party habit with no recorded inventor.
aruba-ariba: The Aruba Ariba was created on 1 July 1963 by Juan 'Jocky' Tromp, the 24-year-old bar manager of the Aruba Caribbean Hotel, now the Hilton, who won a bartenders' competition with it. Its signature ingredient is coecoei, an Aruban liqueur made from the sap of a local agave mixed with rum and sugar, and the drink became the most popular mixed drink of the island's tourist trade. The hotel still marks the anniversary each July.
bundy-and-coke: Bundy and Coke is Queensland's everyday rum highball, Bundaberg rum topped with cola, and nobody has a recorded claim to having mixed the first one.
fluffy-duck: The Fluffy Duck is a creamy advocaat and gin cocktail long loved in Australia, though who first mixed it, and where, is not recorded.
jagertee: Jagertee, hunter's tea, is the hot tea-and-rum drink of Austria's mountain huts, a custom with no recorded inventor whose name is now protected in the EU for spirit drinks from Austria.
wei-er-spritzer: The Weißer Spritzer, white wine lengthened with sparkling water, is Vienna's everyday drink, and like most simple habits it has no recorded inventor.
goombay-smash: The Goombay Smash is credited to Emily Cooper, who ran Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar in New Plymouth on Green Turtle Cay in the Abacos. Accounts place its creation in the 1960s or the early 1970s, and by most of them Miss Emily never drank alcohol herself. The bar stayed in her family, which has kept the exact recipe to itself, and the name echoes goombay, the drum-led music of the Bahamas.
sky-juice: Sky juice is a Bahamian mix of gin, coconut water and condensed milk sold at Nassau's roadside stands, a local favourite with no recorded inventor.
yellow-bird: The Yellow Bird is a Caribbean rum and Galliano drink whose inventor is not recorded, though it shares its name with the popular island song.
bajan-rum-punch: Barbados is often named as the birthplace of rum: English colonists there were distilling a fierce cane spirit they called kill-devil by the middle of the seventeenth century. Punch, a mix of spirit, citrus, sugar, water and spice that English sailors and traders brought back from India, followed it into the island's taverns. The rhyme used to make it, one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong and four of weak, has no known author, and Jamaica claims a version for its planter's punch as firmly as Barbados claims it for its own.
corn-n-oil: Corn 'n' oil is a Barbadian mix of dark rum and falernum, the island's spiced lime syrup, and neither its inventor nor the origin of its name is recorded.
krambambula: The name comes from Krambambuli, a red cherry liqueur once made by the Der Lachs distillery in Danzig, now Gdańsk, whose name lived on in German student song. How it came to mean a hot Belarusian drink of honey, spice and spirit is not documented, though it is now widely treated as a Belarusian national drink and is also sold bottled.
half-en-half: The half-en-half belongs to the cafés around the Brussels stock exchange, where, the story goes, traders who had lost money ordered half white wine and half sparkling wine while the winners drank champagne. Its best-known home is Le Cirio on the Rue de la Bourse, the café founded by the Italian food entrepreneur Francesco Cirio, which still pours it as its house drink.
maitrank: Maitrank, May drink, is white wine steeped with sweet woodruff, a springtime custom of the Arlon area in Belgian Luxembourg, with no recorded inventor.
panty-ripper: The panty ripper is Belize's popular mix of coconut rum and pineapple juice, and neither its inventor nor the source of its cheeky name is recorded.
rum-swizzle: Bermuda's rum swizzle is most closely tied to the Swizzle Inn in Bailey's Bay, which dates its first swizzle to 1932 and calls itself the home of the drink, under the motto Swizzle Inn, Swagger Out. The swizzle itself is older and Caribbean: drinks were churned over ice with a stick cut from a tree whose branches end in a ring of short prongs. Bermuda's version settled on Gosling's rums, falernum and fruit juice, and the island now treats it as its national drink.
chuflay: The chuflay is Bolivia's singani highball, and its name comes with a story rather than a record. British engineers building Bolivia's railways are said to have mixed singani with ginger ale when gin was scarce and called it a short fly, railway slang for a temporary stretch of track laid around an obstacle, which Bolivian ears turned into chuflay. It went on to become a fixture in La Paz, Potosí and Tarija, often served beside a game of cacho, the Bolivian dice game.
yunguenito: The yungueñito is a Bolivian mix of singani and orange juice named for the Yungas valleys northeast of La Paz, and its inventor is not recorded.
batida-de-coco: Batida de coco is the coconut member of Brazil's batida family, whose name means beaten, cachaça blended with coconut milk in a beach-bar staple with no recorded inventor.
caipiroska: The caipiroska is the vodka version of Brazil's caipirinha, a swap so obvious that nobody is recorded as having made it first.
capeta: The capeta, little devil, is a Brazilian mix of cachaça, guaraná and condensed milk associated with the beach towns of the northeast, and its inventor is not recorded.
leite-de-onca: Leite de onça, jaguar's milk, is a creamy cachaça drink from Minas Gerais served at the June festivals, with no recorded inventor.
quentao: Quentão is the hot spiced cachaça of Brazil's Festa Junina, the June festivals of the southern winter, a folk recipe that varies from town to town and has no recorded inventor.
rabo-de-galo: Rabo-de-galo, rooster's tail, is Brazil's mix of cachaça and red vermouth, and its name is usually read as a literal rendering of the English word cocktail, though who first poured it is not recorded.
maple-old-fashioned: The maple Old Fashioned is a modern Canadian twist on the Old Fashioned that swaps sugar for maple syrup, and nobody is recorded as its inventor.
toronto: The Toronto first appears in print as the Fernet Cocktail in Robert Vermeire's 1922 book Cocktails: How to Mix Them, where he noted that it was much appreciated by the Canadians of Toronto. Ontario was under prohibition at the time, so where those Torontonians were drinking it is not recorded. The drink was first printed under the city's name in David Embury's The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks in 1948, and that is the name modern bars use.
borgona: Borgoña, Spanish for Burgundy, is Chile's jug of red wine with strawberries, a home and festival recipe with no recorded inventor.
cola-de-mono: Cola de mono, monkey's tail, is Chile's Christmas drink, and both its beginnings and its name are disputed. The best-known story, told by the historian Belarmino Torres Vergara, has the statesman Pedro Montt, nicknamed El Mono, asking for his Colt revolver as he left a gathering, and his hosts, keen to keep him there, improvising a mix of aguardiente, sugar and milky coffee, so that el Colt de Montt slowly became cola de mono. Another explanation points to the long-tailed monkey on bottles of Spanish Anís del Mono.
piscola: The piscola, Chilean pisco and cola, is Chile's everyday party highball, so simple that nobody is recorded as its inventor.
serena-libre: The Serena libre is a Chilean pisco and papaya drink named for the city of La Serena and the Cuba libre, and its inventor is not recorded.
guihua-jiu: Guihua jiu is Chinese rice wine steeped with osmanthus blossom, a custom with no single recorded beginning that is most at home in Guilin, whose name means osmanthus forest.
warm-huangjiu: Huangjiu has been brewed around Shaoxing for many centuries, and warming it is part of the city's tavern culture. In Lu Xun's short story Kong Yiji, set in the fictional town of Luzhen, modelled on his native Shaoxing, the boy narrator's job at the Xianheng tavern is warming the wine for customers who drink it standing at the counter. Adding ginger or dried plum is a household habit with no recorded inventor, and a common way to serve it in the cold months.
guaro-sour-colombiano: The Colombian guaro sour is aguardiente antioqueño, the anise spirit of Antioquia, shaken with lime and sugar, and its inventor is not recorded.
refajo: Refajo, Colombia's mix of beer and Colombiana soda, is a family-lunch habit whose name means petticoat, and nobody is recorded as its inventor.
chiliguaro: The chiliguaro is a Costa Rican shot of guaro, tomato, lime and hot sauce, a bar favourite whose inventor is not recorded.
guaro-sour: The guaro sour is Costa Rica's simplest way with guaro, the national cane spirit, mixed with lime and sugar, and its inventor is not recorded.
bevanda: Bevanda, red wine cut with water, is the everyday drink of Dalmatia, and its name is simply the Italian word for a drink; nobody recorded when the habit began.
gemist: Gemišt, from the German for mixed, is Croatia's white wine and sparkling water, an everyday habit with no recorded inventor.
canchanchara: By Cuban tradition the canchánchara goes back to the mambises, the fighters of the nineteenth-century wars of independence against Spain, who are said to have mixed aguardiente with honey and whatever citrus they had, and drunk it hot in the countryside. It survived mainly in oral tradition until late in the twentieth century, when people restoring the colonial centre of Trinidad revived it, and the town's La Canchánchara tavern, where it is served in small clay cups, made it a local emblem.
el-presidente: El Presidente became a Havana favourite in the years of American Prohibition, and both its inventor and its namesake are disputed. Some accounts place an early version at the Vista Alegre café as early as 1915 and name it for President Mario García Menocal; others credit Eddie Woelke, an American bartender who came to Havana around 1920, and tie the name to Menocal or to Gerardo Machado, president from 1925. Writing in 1928, Basil Woon called it the aristocrat of cocktails, the drink favoured by well-to-do Cubans.
havana-special: The Havana Special is a Cuban rum, pineapple and maraschino sour from the Havana cocktail era, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.
mary-pickford: The Mary Pickford comes from Havana in the 1920s, when American Prohibition sent drinkers to Cuba, and is named for the silent-film star, who visited the city in those years. Basil Woon's 1928 book When It's Cocktail Time in Cuba credits it to Fred Kaufman, a bartender at the Hotel Sevilla-Biltmore. Some later writers name Eddie Woelke of the Jockey Club instead, so who mixed it first is still argued over, though the earlier printed account names Kaufman.
mulata: The mulata is a Havana rum sour with crème de cacao, usually linked to the Floridita bar, though its creator and date are not firmly recorded.
saoco: Saoco is the old Cuban habit of mixing rum with coconut water, often in the coconut itself, a country drink with no recorded inventor.
beton: The Beton was created in 1967 for Expo 67 in Montreal, where it was served as a refreshment at the Czechoslovak pavilion. Its name joins the start of Becherovka to the end of tonic, and is also the Czech word for concrete. Becherovka itself is much older: Josef Becher began selling the herbal bitter in Karlovy Vary in 1807, from a recipe he is said to have worked out with Christian Frobrig, an English physician visiting the spa.
s-nderjysk-kaffepunch: Sønderjysk kaffepunch, coffee with schnapps and sugar, belongs to the coffee-table traditions of Southern Jutland, and its beginnings are not recorded.
santo-libre: The Santo libre is the Dominican Republic's rum and lemon-lime soda, its name a nod to the Cuba libre, and nobody is recorded as its inventor.
canelazo: Canelazo is the hot cinnamon and aguardiente drink of the Ecuadorian and Colombian Andes, sold at festivals and street stalls, and its inventor is not recorded.
millimallikas: Millimallikas, Estonian for jellyfish, is a layered shot of sambuca and cream liqueur named for the tendrils it forms, and its inventor is not recorded.
vana-tallinn-coffee: Vana Tallinn, the liqueur at the heart of this coffee, was created in 1960 in Soviet-era Tallinn by the master distiller Ilse Maar, the bottling manager Bernhard Jürno and the distillery specialist Jaan Siimo, and it has been made by Liviko ever since. Estonians have long added the liqueur, with its rum base, citrus and vanilla, to coffee and hot chocolate, though no one is recorded as having first poured it into coffee with cream.
tej: Tej has no recorded beginning, and much of its history comes from the accounts of visitors. Francisco Álvares, a priest who reached the Ethiopian court with a Portuguese embassy in the early sixteenth century, described honey wine at royal feasts, and a century later the Jesuit Jerónimo Lobo noted that it was thought discourteous not to offer it to guests. For much of its history tej was brewed in noble households and drunk at court, before spreading to the tej houses of towns and cities.
lonkero: The lonkero was born for the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, when Finland's state alcohol monopoly wanted something quick to serve foreign visitors and, with the drinks company Hartwall, introduced ready-mixed long drinks of gin with grapefruit soda and of brandy with Pommac. The gin version outlived the Games and became a national habit, while the brandy one was dropped. Its name is the English long drink bent to Finnish pronunciation, and lonkero also happens to be the Finnish word for tentacle.
salmiakki-shot: Salmiakki vodka spread through Finnish bars in the early 1990s, when bartenders began dissolving salty liquorice, flavoured with ammonium chloride, into vodka, and there is no settled account of who did it first. Alko, the state alcohol monopoly, put a bottled version, Salmiakki Koskenkorva, known as Salmari, on sale for the New Year of 1993 and withdrew it that March amid concern over its popularity with young people. It returned to the shelves in 1995 and became one of Finland's best-known flavoured spirits.
absinthe-drip: Absinthe began in the Val-de-Travers in western Switzerland, where legend credits a French doctor, Pierre Ordinaire, with the recipe and where Major Dubied opened the first absinthe distillery at Couvet in 1797, joined by Henri-Louis Pernod, who later built a second one at Pontarlier in France. The drip, iced water poured slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon until the spirit clouds into its milky louche, became the ritual of nineteenth-century French cafés, where early evening was called l'heure verte, the green hour.
blue-lagoon: Harry's New York Bar in Paris claims the Blue Lagoon, and the usual credit goes to Andy MacElhone, son of the bar's long-time owner Harry MacElhone, in the 1960s, though some accounts place it later. Its colour comes from blue curaçao, an orange liqueur dyed a vivid blue, and that colour has kept it on holiday menus ever since.
champs-elysees: The Champs-Élysées takes its name from the Paris avenue and was in print by 1925, in Nina Toye and A. H. Adair's book Drinks, Long and Short. Harry Craddock gave it a wider audience in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, where it appears scaled up as a batch for six, but who first mixed it, and where, is not recorded.
communard: The Communard, red wine with crème de cassis, is the red cousin of the Kir, named for the Paris Commune and also called a Cardinal, and its inventor is not recorded.
kir: The Kir takes its name from Canon Félix Kir, a priest and wartime Resistance figure who was mayor of Dijon from 1945 until his death, and who served blanc-cassis, white Burgundy with blackcurrant liqueur, at receptions for visiting delegations, especially those of the town-twinning movement he championed. The drink itself was older, a café mix made popular by the commercial cassis Dijon had produced since 1841, and Kir let local producers use his name, so it spread as his.
mauresque: The mauresque, Moorish in French, is pastis softened with orgeat, one of the colour-coded pastis drinks of southern France, and its inventor is not recorded.
monaco: The Monaco, lager with lemonade and grenadine, is a French café order from the same family as the panaché, and nobody is recorded as its inventor.
monkey-gland: The Monkey Gland is Harry MacElhone's, and its name came from the headlines: he printed it in his 1922 book Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails as his own invention, named after Voronoff's experiments in rejuvenation. Serge Voronoff, a Russian-born surgeon working in France, was then famous for grafting slices of monkey testicle into men in the hope of restoring their youth, a treatment later discredited. The drink is usually linked with Harry's New York Bar in Paris, which MacElhone bought in 1923, and it crossed to London, where it appears in The Savoy Cocktail Book.
perroquet: The perroquet, parrot in French, is pastis turned green with mint syrup, one of the colour-coded pastis drinks of Marseille and the south, and its inventor is not recorded.
picon-biere: Picon bière starts with Amer Picon, the bitter orange aperitif created by Gaétan Picon, a Frenchman who had served with the army in Algeria and set up production there before opening a factory in Marseille. Drinkers in eastern and northern France took to pouring a measure of it into their beer, and the pairing became the standard way to drink Picon there, though nobody recorded who did it first.
rose: The Rose is credited to Johnny Mitta, the barman at the Chatham Hotel in Paris, and it was one of the city's fashionable drinks in the 1920s, when Prohibition sent American drinkers across the Atlantic to its bars. Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar printed a recipe for it in his 1927 book Barflies and Cocktails.
tomate: The tomate is pastis reddened with grenadine, named for its colour rather than any tomato, one of the colour-coded pastis drinks of Provence, with no recorded inventor.
berliner-weisse-mit-schuss: Berliner Weisse is old and its origins are argued over: some trace it to the sixteenth-century brewer Cord Broihan's copy of a Hamburg beer, others to Huguenot refugees, and one early record puts its brewing in Berlin in 1572. By the late nineteenth century it was the city's most popular alcoholic drink, and the claim that Napoleon's soldiers called it the Champagne of the North is a popular story rather than a documented fact. The Schuss, a shot of raspberry or woodruff syrup to soften its sourness, is how most drinkers now meet it, in a wide bowl glass.
feuerzangenbowle: Feuerzangenbowle, fire-tongs punch, is named for the tongs once used to hold a rum-soaked sugarloaf over a bowl of mulled wine while it burned, and German student fraternities have also called it Krambambuli since the nineteenth century. Its fame came from Heinrich Spoerl's comic novel of the same name and above all the wartime film adaptation starring Heinz Rühmann, which German universities still screen in the weeks before Christmas, sometimes to thousands of viewers.
gluhwein: Hot spiced wine was drunk across Europe long before anyone called it Glühwein, and the German custom has a famous early relic: a lockable, gold-plated silver tankard attributed to Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen, a fifteenth-century nobleman whose cellar records hold the earliest known mention of Riesling, is described as the oldest documented Glühwein tankard. The drink became the scent of the Christmas markets of Germany, Austria and Alsace, and EU law now defines it as made from wine alone, sweetened and spiced, with no water added.
kalte-ente: Kalte Ente, cold duck, is usually traced to a legend about Prince Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, the last Elector of Trier, who is said to have ordered the unfinished wine of an evening mixed with sparkling wine rather than wasted. The mix was supposedly called kaltes Ende, the cold end, which drifted into kalte Ente. In Detroit after Prohibition, Harold Borgman of Pontchartrain Wine Cellars borrowed the name for an American Cold Duck of champagne and sparkling burgundy, a different drink from the German original.
lumumba: Lumumba, hot chocolate with rum or brandy, is drunk in Germany and parts of northern Europe, and its name is assumed to refer to Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of independent Congo, though nobody has documented who chose it or why.
